Dominic
DOM-uh-nik
proper noun
Dominic de Guzmán (c. 1170–1221), founder of the Order of Preachers; from the Latin dominicus, “of the Lord.”

Biblical Definition

Dominic de Guzmán was a Spanish priest of the early thirteenth century who founded the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans, devoted to learned preaching and the defense of Catholic doctrine against the Albigensian heresy of southern France. The honorable part of his work the dictionary will name plainly: in an age when many clergy were idle and ignorant, Dominic insisted that the church needed trained, disciplined preachers who could expound and contend for the faith, and his order produced great minds, Thomas Aquinas among them, and labored for the spread of doctrine and learning. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God; an order built to preach answered a real lack. Yet the dictionary cannot honor Dominic as a faithful witness without naming the corruptions bound up in his work and his order. The crusade against the Albigenses, however genuinely the Cathar heresy needed answering, was prosecuted by the sword and folded into the machinery of the medieval Inquisition that the Dominicans came to staff. And the rosary devotion long ascribed to Dominic enshrines the Marian piety that corrupts the one mediation of Christ. Dominic’s zeal for preaching and doctrine the dictionary honors; the inquisitorial sword and the Marian devotion it names as the corruptions of the medieval church the Reformation called the church away from.

Webster 1828 Definition

Founder of the Dominican Order of Preachers (c. 1170–1221); honored for his zeal for trained preaching, named for the inquisitorial sword and Marian devotion of his tradition.

DOMINIC (c. 1170–1221), founder of the Order of Preachers (Dominicans).

Insisted the church needed learned, disciplined preachers against heresy.

His order produced great minds, including Thomas Aquinas.

Bound up with the crusade against the Albigenses and the medieval Inquisition.

The rosary devotion ascribed to him enshrines a Marian piety that corrupts Christ’s sole mediation.

Key Scripture

Rom 10:14 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"

2Ti 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

1Ti 2:5 — "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;"

Col 2:8 — "Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ."

Modern Corruption

The Dominican zeal for preaching is honored, but the inquisitorial sword against heresy and the Marian rosary devotion are corruptions of the gospel the Reformation recovered.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is not Dominic’s call to preach but the means and the piety his order carried. The crusade and inquisition against the Albigenses answered heresy with the magistrate’s sword wielded by the church, confusing the two kingdoms and persecuting conscience—the very abuse the Reformers and the Baptist confessions would later renounce. And the rosary, long tied to Dominic’s name, directs prayer to Mary as a mediatrix and intercessor, corrupting the one mediation of the man Christ Jesus, who alone stands between God and men. Devotion to the saints and to the Virgin, however sincere, robs Christ of His sole office.

The principle to recover is preaching that contends for the faith by the Word and not by the sword, and prayer offered through the one Mediator alone. Faith comes by hearing the word of God; heresy is answered by sound doctrine, not by the inquisitor’s fire. And there is one God and one Mediator; to Him alone the church prays, casting down every devotion that would set another intercessor beside the Son.

Hebrew Roots

Founder of the Dominicans (c. 1170–1221); honored for learned preaching, named for the inquisitorial sword and Marian devotion.

Dominic — founder of the Order of Preachers (c. 1170–1221).

Insisted on trained preachers against heresy (Rom 10:14).

His order produced Thomas Aquinas and much learning.

Bound up with the crusade and Inquisition against the Albigenses.

One Mediator, Christ alone, answers the Marian rosary (1Ti 2:5).

Usage

"Dominic founded an order built to preach and contend for doctrine."

"The Inquisition the Dominicans staffed answered heresy with the sword."

"The rosary ascribed to him corrupts the one mediation of Christ."
